37561:
1 John has no greeting or farewell; it reads like a sermon or circular tract. It moves in spirals rather than straight lines, returning again and again to the same themes from new angles: walking in the light, confessing sin, keeping commands, loving fellow believers, and confessing Jesus rightly.

The crisis was a schism. The writer calls those who left 'antichrists' and 'false prophets'. Their exact teaching is reconstructed from the writer's replies: they seem to have denied that the human Jesus was the Messiah and Son of God, or that Christ came 'in the flesh' and 'by water and blood' (that is, truly lived and truly died). This fits early forms of docetism (from Greek dokeo, 'to seem'), the idea that Christ only seemed to be human. Irenaeus tells of a teacher in Asia, Cerinthus, who taught that the divine Christ descended on the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross, and of a story that John fled a bathhouse when Cerinthus entered.

The split was also moral and relational. Those who left apparently claimed fellowship with God and freedom from sin while neglecting love for poorer believers. The writer insists that knowing God cannot be separated from obeying him and caring for a brother or sister in need.
37563: Believers are 'children of God', 'brothers and sisters', 'little children'. In a collectivist world, family meant obligation: you share your goods with kin. Refusing help to a sibling in need denies the family bond.
37565: Jesus is the hilasmos for sins, a word used in the Greek Old Testament for atonement rites. It recalls the Day of Atonement, where God himself provides the means of cleansing.
37567: A parakletos was a supporter who stood beside someone in court. Jesus is the righteous advocate with the Father.
37569: Early churches received travelling prophets and teachers. Like Deuteronomy's tests of prophets, John gives a test: confession of Jesus come in the flesh.
37571: The closing warning, 'keep yourselves from idols', fits a city full of temples (Artemis, the emperors) and may also mean any false picture of God.
37572:
Although the readers were likely a mixed community in a Greek city, 1 John's world is deeply Jewish. God is light, as the Psalms and Isaiah proclaim. The 'old commandment' they have had from the beginning is the command of love, rooted in Leviticus 19:18 and renewed by Jesus. Cain, who killed his brother, is the negative example of hatred within the family. Sin is defined as 'lawlessness' (anomia), the breaking of God's covenant instruction. The atoning sacrifice language comes straight from Israel's temple worship.

The writer's 'tests' are covenantal, not anxious checklists. In Israel's covenant, God's gracious initiative came first ('we love because he first loved us') and faithfulness followed: knowing God meant walking in his ways, as Jeremiah said of King Josiah, 'he judged the cause of the poor; was not this to know me?' A Jewish-rooted hearer would hear 1 John as saying that the God of Israel has revealed himself in the flesh of Jesus the Messiah, and that the community that confesses him must look like its Father: truthful, righteous and loving toward the vulnerable.

37641:
2 John is the shortest book in the New Testament, short enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus. It follows the normal pattern of an ancient letter: sender, recipient, greeting, main body, hope to visit, greetings from others.

Its setting is the network of house churches that early Christians relied on. There were no church buildings; believers met in homes. Teachers and missionaries travelled from town to town and depended on hospitality, as did the elder's own messengers. This network was how the gospel spread, but it also allowed false teachers to move around. The Didache, an early Christian manual, gives practical rules: a true prophet does not stay more than two days or ask for money.

The specific danger was the same as in 1 John: teachers who did not confess 'Jesus Christ coming in the flesh'. The elder calls them deceivers and 'the antichrist', and says those who 'run ahead' beyond the teaching of Christ do not have God.
37642: Receiving a guest into the home meant food, lodging and public endorsement. In a house church, welcoming a teacher also gave him a platform to teach the whole congregation.
37644: Kyria ('lady') could be a woman's name or title, but the language of her 'children' and her 'elect sister' suggests sister congregations, as Israel and Jerusalem were pictured as a mother or bride.
37646: Letters opened with greetings and closed with wishes to visit 'face to face' ('mouth to mouth'), since writing was a poor substitute for presence.
37648: To 'greet' a person publicly signalled honour and fellowship. Refusing the greeting was a public statement of distance.
37649:
The elder's main command is the 'commandment we have had from the beginning, that we love one another', the Torah's love command renewed by Jesus. 'Walking' in truth and in the commandments is Jewish halakhic language (halakhah means 'walking'), describing a way of life shaped by God's instruction. The picture of a community as a 'lady' and her 'children' echoes the prophets' images of Zion as mother of her people.

The warning against receiving false teachers also follows a Jewish pattern: Deuteronomy commanded Israel not to listen to prophets who led the people after other gods, however impressive their signs. For a first-century audience the issue was covenant loyalty. To deny that the Messiah came in the flesh was to deny the God who sent him, and to support such teaching would be to share in its work.

37680: One who leads astray, a misleader.

37704:
3 John is the most personal letter in the New Testament after Philemon, and about the same length as 2 John. It gives a rare, ground-level glimpse of early church life: missionaries travelling 'for the sake of the Name', relying on believers for food, lodging and supplies for the next stage of the journey; letters of recommendation; and a power struggle in a local congregation.

Diotrephes may have been the host of a house church, which in the ancient world gave the householder considerable control over who could attend and teach. Some scholars see in the conflict an early stage of the shift from travelling leadership to strong local leaders (later bishops); others see a simple clash of personality and pride. The elder does not accuse Diotrephes of false teaching, only of love of status, slander and refusing hospitality.

The missionaries took nothing from 'the Gentiles' (here meaning unbelievers), so they relied entirely on believers' generosity. Supporting them made the host a 'fellow worker for the truth'.
37706: Hosts acted as patrons to travelling teachers, and support was expected 'in a manner worthy of God'. Hospitality was a central Jewish and early Christian virtue, modelled by Abraham.
37708: Philoproteuo ('love to be first') describes the competitive pursuit of honour that dominated ancient social life. Jesus taught the reverse: the first must be servant of all.
37710: Travellers carried letters vouching for them to hosts. The elder's commendation of Demetrius functions as such a letter.
37712: Greek letters routinely opened with a wish for the recipient's health and well-being, much like 'I hope this finds you well'.
37714: Going out 'for the sake of the Name' echoes Jewish reverence for God's Name and Jesus' teaching about suffering for his name.
37715:
Hospitality to travellers was a deep Jewish virtue. Abraham ran to welcome strangers at Mamre; Torah commanded love for the stranger because Israel had been strangers in Egypt; and Jewish communities across the diaspora hosted travelling teachers and messengers. Gaius stands in that tradition. Walking 'in the truth' again reflects the Jewish idea of life as a walk in God's ways.

The elder's advice, 'do not imitate what is evil but what is good', sounds like the wisdom tradition's two ways. Diotrephes' fault is the opposite of covenant humility: hoarding honour rather than serving God's messengers. For a first audience, the letter would have been heard as a practical application of covenant faithfulness in a small community: open doors, generous provision and humble leadership.
